So I did a little quick research and it appears I have been a bit mistaken. Here's an article I found:

http://journals.humankinetics.com/AcuCustom/Sitename/Documents/DocumentItem/2115.pdf

From what I gather the key importance is that you are doing ab crunches and not full sit-ups. If your hip flexors take over and do the work then your range of motions is too great. Don't go above 45 degrees angle from the floor, because that's when you start getting lumbar spine flexion. The relevant part I found is on page 18 (page 8/10 in the pdf I think). Key snippet:

"The trunk curl sit-up with the hips and knees flexed requires the highest lumbar spine flexion when performed correctly. Conversely, the standard abdominal crunch as previously described by several authors (10,25,26) does not cause flexion of the lumbar spine and has been found to be a superior isometric exercise".

I was going to say, crunches are fine, it's full sit ups that wreck you. Especially if you yank on the back of your head.

My recommendation? Frog sit-ups. Sit down on the floor, with feet touching and splayed out to the sides. If your feet cannot touch no biggie, but still have them splayed out so you almost make a diamond with your legs and feet. Then put your fingertips together over your head so that they are touching, like making a point. Lay back carefully and make sure your hands touch the ground above/behind your head. From that position, come back to a sitting position, but continue forward until your hands/fingertips touch a point beyond your feet(while keeping your legs/feet in a diamond position). That is a single repetition.

The exercise pretty much ensured you aren't using any aids when working your core, minus some momentum(if you need it) from your arms.

Example here: http://www.top.me/single_exercise/frog-sit-ups

In the example he doesn't come all the way forward and touch the floor in front of him, but I kind of recommend it because it goes beyond the point of work for your abdominals and so can give you a little rest(since you are working on rebuilding).

I also recommend the plank, both side and standard as well as the leg lift (lying down and hanging)

So from what I gather you have a barbell but no rack or anything like that? That's what I'm going to assume so bear with me.

What I would do in your situation is a pretty basic push/pull split four times a week. That's monday push, wednesday pull, friday push, sunday pull. Or however you wanna do it.

On push day I would do military press 5 sets of 5 reps, landmine press 5 sets of 5 reps, pushups (from your knees if you have to) in whatever configuration works from your level, and barbell squats. Back squats if you have some form of rack or front squats so you can pick up the bar from the ground. 5 sets of 5 reps. Finnish off with hip thrusts for that booty. Everyone loves a good booty. I would probably go 5 sets of 12 reps.

The important thing here is to mind your shoulders. Don't push through the pain when it comes to your shoulders. It's a weak joint and it takes a while to recover if you damage it. Just be mindful and you'll be all right.

On pull day I would do T-bar rows 5x5, Australian pull ups however many you can manage(since you don't have much upper body strength you need to build that up before jumping into pull ups), some bicep curls, and finnish of with deadlifts 3 sets of 5.
